newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia wheat trade sees 1996 price surge repeat.
newsitem.headline: Australia wheat trade sees 1996 price surge repeat.

text.p: Australian brokers and analysts see the potential for a repeat of the dramatic wheat price rise of almost exactly a year ago but some pass off current world grain market jitters as seasonal panic.
These views come on the eve of the latest USDA crop update in the U.S. as markets tensely look for direction after recent weather scares.

Low world wheat stocks and uncertain weather around the wheat-producing world had created the same set of forces which this time last year sent wheat prices rocketing to about A$250.00 a tonne, Mark Martin, managing director of rural consultancy Agracom Risk Management, said.
"Prices rose from US$5.00 a bushel last year to $6.50 in three weeks on tight supply scares, when ending stocks were predicted to be 105.5 million tonnes," Martin said.
"We now have prices of $4.50 with the potential for ending stocks lower than 100 million tonnes. It's highly conceivable we could see a similar rally to ... last year," he said.
Australian wheat prices now stand at about A$190.00 a tonne in nearby Sydney Futures Exchange contracts and A$198.00 on the Australian Wheat Board's 1997/98 national indicator price.
The world wheat price reached its high-point at about the present time in 1996, reaching at least US$6.50 a bushel, or more than A$250.00 a tonne in Sydney Futures Exchange contracts.

This year world wheat ending stocks for 1996/97 had been revised down to 108 million tonnes from 112 million tonnes by the USDA in early April, but frost and flood in the U.S. and drought in Europe have figures on a likely continued downward spiral, Martin said.
The next two weeks would be critical for drought-stricken wheat areas in both Europe and Australia, he said.
But Martin sees dry conditions in Europe, frost and floods in the U.S. and Australia's current dry combining to reduce world ending stocks to about 96 million tonnes overall.
Some brokers agree, others do not.
"We would agree with that (for) a short sharp rally in the grains market," Gary Booth of Ord Minnett Jardine Fleming said.
In an absolutely weather-driven market, Australia's Southern Oscillation Index continued to plunge, indicating more dry conditions in the southeast seaboard, he said.
While some time remained before matters became critical, "each week becomes tighter and more difficult," he said.
Brendan Hillary of ANZ Futures Ltd, a sceptic on scares, said he waited on the USDA progress report on spring wheat, due out after Monday's Chicago close.
And although U.S. planting was a long way behind average, last year's performance showed that a lot of wheat was able to be put in in a very short period of time, he said.

"I think it'll be fine. Everyone panics this time of year." Hillary also pointed out that much-awaited rain fell this weekend in France, enough to satisfy immediate needs, although follow-up rain would be needed in the next 10-14 days.

"Basically until the U.S. gets the spring wheat crop in, we're probably going to hover up around these (price) levels. If there's any hiccup in production during the crop going into the ground we'll see a little upside in price.
"Otherwise, (the present market has) a pretty good price for this time of year and things will head down to their normal seasonality, if the (U.S.) crop goes in.
"Normally speaking, when damage comes into the marketplace they always over-estimate it," Hillary said.
"The damage estimates would appear to be coming into the lower end now, whereas the middle of last week it was definitely going to be a total wipeout," he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
